country_findings.statement: Egypt already has a large, geographically-defined smallholder targeting frame in place: the IFAD-financed Sustainable Transformation for Agricultural Resilience in Upper Egypt (STAR) project, executed by the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation with USD 269.64 million total financing, targets 160,000 rural households in about 160 villages across Minya, Assiut and Sohag governorates, and its 2025 supervision mission included a Global Technical Specialist on ICT for Development (ICT4D). A digital agriculture roadmap chapter on priority regions and farmer segments can anchor its Upper Egypt smallholder targeting on this existing beneficiary cohort rather than defining a new one.
country_findings.quote: STAR’s objective is to improve the income and resilience of smallholder and landless families for 160,000 rural HHs in about 160 villages as direct beneficiaries in Minya, Assiut and Sohag Governorates.
country_findings.why_it_matters: Chapter 3 must name priority regions and farmer segments. This is a live, government-executed programme with an explicit, quantified beneficiary definition (smallholder and landless households) and named governorates (Minya, Assiut, Sohag) running to 2029, so digital use cases for Upper Egypt smallholders can be sequenced against an already-financed delivery channel and an already-identified population, avoiding a parallel targeting exercise. The mission's inclusion of an ICT4D technical specialist further signals an existing entry point for digital components within this targeting frame.
country_findings.source_name: IFAD, Egypt — Sustainable Transformation for Agricultural Resilience in Upper Egypt, Supervision Report No. 7424-EG (mission 19/10/2025–16/11/2025)

country_findings.statement: Egypt's public agricultural spending is overwhelmingly directed to producer/consumer price support rather than to the general-services budget line where a digital agriculture programme would normally sit: OECD reports that support to general services was only 2.6% of the value of agricultural production in 2022-24, and that this envelope is already dominated by irrigation infrastructure (76%) and agricultural R&D (14%), leaving roughly a tenth of a very small envelope for everything else — including information systems, extension, inspection and market data. Any costed digital programme therefore has to be routed either as an incremental claim on an unusually thin GSSE envelope, as a rider on irrigation investment (the dominant recipient), or through external/partner finance, and the roadmap's envelope scenarios should be sized against that structural constraint rather than against total agricultural support (2.8% of GDP in 2022-24, the highest of the 54 countries in the OECD's Agricultural Support database).
country_findings.quote: Support to general services (GSSE) amounted to 2.6% of the value of agricultural production in 2022-24. This was dominated by investments in irrigation infrastructure (76% of total GSSE expenditures), followed by expenditures on agricultural R&D (14%).
country_findings.why_it_matters: Chapter 5 must route costs to real budget instruments. This tells the drafter the size and composition of the only public budget line that can plausibly host digital agriculture spending (GSSE), that irrigation infrastructure crowds it out, and that headline 'high support to agriculture' figures are misleading as an indicator of fiscal space for digital public goods — a fact no maturity indicator would reveal.
country_findings.source_name: OECD, Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt — Chapter 2: Trends and evaluation of agricultural policy in Egypt

country_findings.statement: Egypt already has a national farmer registry instrument — the agricultural holding system known as the Farmer's Card — and its expansion is an explicit target in the FY 2025/2026 government development plan, with the plan aiming for 80% of holdings to be covered; any sequenced digital investment program should treat this registry build-out as the upstream dependency (identity/holding data) for downstream services such as contract farming (targeted at 1.8 million feddans) and subsidy or extension delivery, with the Ministry of Planning, Economic Development and International Cooperation as the plan owner presenting the targets to the House of Representatives and MALR/MWRI as implementing ministries.
country_findings.quote: in addition to developing the agricultural holding system (Farmer's Card) to reach a beneficiary holding ratio of 80%
country_findings.why_it_matters: A chapter on sequencing needs to know what foundational registry already exists and who owns it, rather than proposing a new farmer database. The Farmer's Card is a government-owned, budgeted, target-bearing instrument inside the annual development plan, so it is the natural anchor for sequencing: registry coverage first, then contractual agriculture (1.8 million feddans), irrigation modernisation and extension digitalisation layered on top. A maturity indicator would score 'farmer registry exists' but would not reveal the coverage target, the fiscal year commitment, the EGP 17.5 billion agriculture-and-irrigation envelope it sits within, or that the accountability line runs through the Ministry of Planning to Parliament.
country_findings.source_name: Ministry of International Cooperation (Egypt) — "Minister of Planning, Economic Development and International Cooperation Reviews Targets of the Agriculture and Irrigation Sectors in the FY 2025/2026 Development Plan before the House of Representatives"

country_findings.statement: Egypt already has a large World Bank-financed operation whose stated development objective covers both climate-smart agriculture adoption and the national agricultural information and early warning system — the Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (P180480), a US$250 million IBRD Investment Project Financing implemented by the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, so the roadmap's climate-alignment chapter should build on (and avoid duplicating) this existing vehicle for advisory and weather/climate data investment.
country_findings.quote:
To foster the adoption of CSA technologies and practices in the project area and to strengthen the nation-wide
agriculture information system and early warning services
country_findings.why_it_matters: Maturity indicators would score the reach of advisory services or the state of weather/climate data, but would not reveal that a specific, already-approved US$250 million financing arrangement with named implementing ministries exists whose objective is precisely to strengthen the nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services alongside CSA adoption. A drafter needs this to anchor Chapter 8 actions in an existing budgeted programme, identify the institutional owners (MWRI, MoE, MALR under the Ministry of International Cooperation), and target roadmap activities at gaps the project does not cover rather than re-proposing the same investment.
country_findings.source_name: World Bank — Project Information Document (Concept Stage), Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (P180480), Egypt, Arab Republic of

country_findings.statement: Any policy or legal-drafting work for Egypt's digital agriculture roadmap must be designed around an already fragmented institutional mandate: agricultural and food policy is split across the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade, and the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation (plus other ministries for trade, rural development and environment), which the OECD identifies as a source of co-ordination and implementation problems. Reform actions therefore need an explicit inter-ministerial co-ordination instrument and clear assignment of legal authority, rather than assuming a single lead ministry can enact digital-agriculture rules.
country_findings.quote: Responsibilities for agricultural and food policies in Egypt fall across different ministries and agencies, creating challenges for policy co-ordination and implementation. The Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade, and The Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation all oversee some agricultural policies. Other ministries and agencies play important roles related to trade, rural development or the environment.
country_findings.why_it_matters: Maturity indicators can score whether a data-governance or digital-agriculture policy exists, but they will not reveal that the mandate to draft and enforce it is divided across at least three ministries. This determines who must sign a legal instrument, where a digital agriculture governance body should sit, and why past reform attempts stalled — all decisions the policy and safeguards chapter must make up front.
country_findings.source_name: OECD, Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt (OECD Agriculture and Food Policy Reviews), Chapter 2: Trends and evaluation of agricultural policy in Egypt

country_findings.statement: The Economic Affairs Sector of Egypt's Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation (MALR) — the sector formally tasked with publishing data on Egypt's agricultural activities — already declares as its official vision the digitalization of Egyptian agriculture for sustainable agricultural development within the framework of Egypt Vision 2030 and national/international statistical data-system concepts. This gives a drafting team a named, existing institutional home with a published digital mandate rooted in the statistical function, rather than a new body needing creation.
country_findings.quote: رقمنة الزراعة المصرية لتحقيق تنمية زراعية مستدامة في إطار رؤية مصر 2030، وفي ضوء المفاهيم  القومية والدولية لنظم البيانات الإحصائية
country_findings.why_it_matters: Chapter 7 must name the mandate holder and institutional home. The Economic Affairs Sector's published vision shows that a digital-agriculture mandate is already lodged inside MALR's statistics/data arm, alongside its stated mission of supporting decision-makers in planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating agricultural development programmes. A roadmap can therefore anchor steering arrangements in an existing unit with an operational data portal (crop map, agricultural censuses, time-series databases, digital publications) rather than proposing a greenfield institution — but it also flags a risk that ownership sits in a statistics sector whose remit is data publication, not cross-cutting service delivery, so steering will need to reach other MALR sectors (e.g. agricultural extension) and MCIT-side actors.
country_findings.source_name: وزارة الزراعة واستصلاح الأراضي – قطاع الشئون الاقتصادية (Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation – Economic Affairs Sector), official website

country_findings.statement: A donor-financed delivery platform with an existing measurement base already exists in Upper Egypt: IFPRI's randomized controlled trial on digital literacy training runs through roughly 30 farmer organizations covering about 4,000 smallholder farmers in Minya and Beni Suef that are supported by GIZ's Agricultural Innovation Project (AIP), and it includes a baseline survey on farmers' access to digital tools and adoption barriers. Chapter 9 can anchor results chains and baselines for digital-tool adoption on this existing RCT and its farmer-organization infrastructure rather than commissioning new baseline measurement from scratch.
country_findings.quote: The target population of our interventions include about 4,000 smallholder farmers located across two governorates in Egypt: Minya and Benisuef. These farmers are part of around 30 farmer organizations in Upper Egypt that are supported by the Agricultural Innovation Project (AIP) of the German Corporation for International Cooperation (GIZ).
country_findings.why_it_matters: A maturity-indicator score would say nothing about which measurement vehicles and delivery partners already exist on the ground. This note identifies a named, donor-financed programme (GIZ AIP), a defined population (about 4,000 smallholders in two governorates), an organisational channel (about 30 farmer organizations), and an experimental design with a baseline survey — all directly reusable as a baseline and monitoring backbone for adoption indicators in the results-and-learning chapter, and as a caution that current evidence is concentrated in Upper Egypt rather than nationally representative.
country_findings.source_name: Abdelaziz, F. and Abay, K.A., "Digital Literacy Training to Promote Diffusion of Digital Agricultural Tools to Smallholder Farmers", IFPRI Policy Note (CGSpace)

country_findings.statement: Egypt already has a horizontal personal-data legal instrument that the digital-agriculture chapter must build on rather than invent: Law No. 151 of 2020 on personal data protection, passed in July 2020, which criminalises processing data outside the purposes authorised by data owners and requires collectors and processors to hold licences, permits and approvals — the baseline for any farmer-data consent, licensing and redress arrangements in the roadmap.
country_findings.quote: It is worth noting that the President of the Republic passed Law No. 151 of 2020 on personal data protection in July 2020. The Law is in line with the best international practices, especially the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
country_findings.why_it_matters: Chapter 10 needs to state where data rights, consent and redress for farmers legally sit. Maturity indicators would score 'data governance' generically; they would not tell a drafter that Egypt has a GDPR-aligned statute (Law 151/2020) whose framework, per the same release, "criminalizes processing data in ways not conforming to the purposes authorized by data owners; and obligates data collectors and processors to obtain the necessary licenses, permits and approvals to conduct their work", nor that a personal data protection centre was to be established to issue those licences. This means agri-data platforms, e-Extension systems and agtech SMEs are regulated entities with licensing and data-protection-officer obligations, and that the safeguards chapter should route farmer consent and redress through this existing regime and its regulator (referred to in later MCIT material as PDPC) instead of proposing a parallel agriculture-only mechanism.
country_findings.source_name: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) — Press Release: MCIT Holds Community Discussions with MNOs, Tech Companies on Personal Data Protection Law Executive Regulations

register_entries.name: El Mufeed in Food and Agriculture (FAO mobile app, Egypt)
register_entries.lead: FAO Representation in Egypt, developed under FAO's Digital Services Portfolio (DSP) and promoted with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation (MALR); rolled out under the project "Inclusive rural Information and communication services for agricultural innovation and resilient family farming in the NENA region"
uc: Advisory content on citrus production
Advisory content on date palm production
Healthy nutrition guidance
Household poultry production guidance
Wholesale price information for vegetables and fruits
COVID-19 food safety information (theme added in 2020)
FAO Egypt news updates pushed to users via an in-app Twitter feed
Free download and use via Google Play Store; used by extension agents to disseminate simplified information to farmers
register_entries.scale: The sources give no user, download or coverage figures. They state only that the app was launched in 2019 nationally in Egypt, that a promotional campaign using social media (Facebook) was run to expand its use and was "recommended for replication in other countries", and that in December 2020 FAO and MALR invited extension agents to use the app and disseminate it among targeted groups.
register_entries.results: No independent evaluation was found in these sources. The only outcome-type material is FAO's own 2023 video of farmer testimonials ("El Mufeed Application in Food and Agriculture: Testimonials") and FAO's self-reported statement that the promotional campaign was successful and recommended for replication — both publisher (FAO) claims about its own app, not independent assessment. No adoption, yield, income or usage metrics are reported.
register_entries.src: FAO Digital Services Portfolio — Country Cases (Egypt)

register_entries.name: EU-ZIRA3A (EU Integrated Rural Development Programme for Egypt)
register_entries.lead: Funded by the European Union (with parallel Italian funding) and implemented by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS Cairo), working with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation (MALR) and governorate directorates
uc: Agricultural extension advice to smallholder farmers via equipped extension departments in Sohag, Assiut and Beni Suef
Veterinary and livestock services, including artificial insemination centres
Irrigation and water-scarcity mitigation support for farmers
Plant quarantine, inspection and sampling services supporting export procedures (visual inspection/sampling of citrus and medicinal and aromatic plants)
Vocational training and income-generating support for rural women and youth
Staff capacity building in data analysis and project management (Excel, Power BI, SPSS) and IT equipment for MALR digital infrastructure
register_entries.scale: Programme website reports a total EU fund of €24M plus AICS parallel funding of €3.3M (one programme news item cites €27.3 million total), covering three governorates — Assiut, Sohag and Beni Suef — with implementation started November 2022 for 66 months; direct beneficiaries described qualitatively as rural farming communities and their cooperatives, with no farmer headcount given. One event report notes the MAPs Festival booth in Beni Suef attracted 'more than 200 visitors'.
register_entries.results: No independent evaluation was found in these sources. The available material is programme/implementer self-reporting (AICS and the EU-ZIRA3A programme website) describing deliveries of IT equipment, trainings and expected results; no outcome data on farmer incomes, yields or service uptake is published here.

register_entries.name: Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (CRAFT), P180480
register_entries.lead: Government of Egypt — borrower Ministry of International Cooperation; implementing agencies Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, Ministry of Environment; financed by the World Bank (IBRD, US$250 million). Part of the food pillar of Egypt's NWFE country platform.
uc: Nation-wide agricultural information system to support farm and policy decision-making
Agro-climatic early warning services for farmers (nationwide component)
Promotion and adoption of climate-smart agriculture technologies and practices
Improved irrigation services and modern (drip/single-lift) irrigation support, including water user associations
Help for smallholders to aggregate and access markets and value chains
Improved access to agricultural finance and technical support
Agricultural risk management and innovation support
register_entries.scale: Total operation cost US$250.00 million, all IBRD financing (World Bank Project Information Document, Concept Stage, 24-Apr-2024). Geographic scope per Egypt's Ministry of International Cooperation (Sept 2024): modern irrigation components in Delta governorates — Menoufia, Sharqia and Gharbia, in centres and villages under the 'Hayah Karima' initiative — and nationwide coverage for the early warning system component; the Minister of Agriculture and Land Reclamation stated the project would benefit 'around 30 million residents' of the Nile Valley and Delta. No farmer-user or registration figures are reported in these sources.
register_entries.results: No independent evaluation was found. The sources are a World Bank concept-stage Project Information Document (April 2024, pre-appraisal) and a September 2024 Egyptian government readout of a preparation-status meeting; neither reports implementation results, adoption rates, or impact evidence.
register_entries.src: World Bank — Project Information Document (Concept Stage), Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (P180480), Report No. PIDC35458

register_entries.name: Digital literacy training to promote diffusion of digital agricultural tools to smallholder farmers (randomized intervention, Egypt)
register_entries.lead: International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Development Strategies and Governance Unit (authors Fatma Abdelaziz and Kibrom A. Abay), implemented with the GIZ Egypt office; funded by the CGIAR Research Program Scaling for Impact and USAID. Registered as AEARCTR-0012723.
uc: Classroom-based digital literacy training for smallholder farmers, delivered through a Training of Trainers (TOT) model
Edutainment variants: a video-based play or a live community play shown before the training, to build awareness and trust
Hands-on onboarding to two Egyptian farmer mobile apps offering crop marketing/sales services
App-based agricultural advisory (extension) information
App-based ordering and delivery of farm inputs
register_entries.scale: The provided sources do not give a farmer or governorate count. They describe only the design: a randomized controlled trial with three treatment arms (T1 standard classroom digital literacy training, T2 training preceded by a video-based play, T3 training preceded by a live community play) and a control group, delivered via a Training of Trainers model and covering two Egyptian mobile apps (IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359, September 2025; Food Policy 141 (2026) 103108). No sample size, number of villages, or budget figure appears in the excerpts available.
register_entries.results: An RCT evaluation by the study authors (IFPRI), published as IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 (Sept 2025) and in the peer-reviewed journal Food Policy 141 (2026) 103108, reports that all variants of digital training significantly increased uptake and utilization of digital tools: the standard digital training alone raised uptake by 20 percentage points and utilization by 26 percentage points (discussion paper) / 18 percentage points (published journal version), and the interventions raised farmer trust in digital tools by 8-13 percentage points. Notably, for some outcomes the training alone outperformed the combined arms that added edutainment nudges, with the authors pointing to group size effects and social influence dynamics during the plays; impacts also varied by farmer gender and age. Caveat: the evaluators are the same team that designed and implemented the intervention (IFPRI with GIZ Egypt), so this is not a third-party evaluation, though the journal version is peer-reviewed.
register_entries.src: IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359, "Digital Literacy Training to Promote Diffusion of Digital Agricultural Tools to Smallholder Farmers: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in Egypt" (September 2025)

register_entries.name: Cultivaet (Cultivaet Platform: Farmer AI Companion, Knowledge Platform, Business SaaS)
register_entries.lead: Cultivaet Technologies Holding Ltd. (private AI/AgriTech startup, founded 2023, HQ Cairo, Egypt; backed by Raya FutureTECH grant and Sanabil 500 MENA Seed Accelerator / 500 Global; Google Cloud Startups Program)
uc: AI farmer assistant giving personalised daily advice based on the farmer's location and crops
Weather forecasts
Crop planning
Pest control guidance
Soil health advice
Knowledge hub collecting and distributing scientific and social agricultural data
B2B SaaS linking farmers to food-industry buyers for funding, purchase and procurement with traceability
register_entries.scale: No user or farmer reach figures are reported in any source. Company size only: "3 employees" per the Pitch directory profile [2]; "11-50 employees" per LinkedIn [4] and Lucidity Insights [6]. Funding stage reported by Lucidity Insights as a grant (Raya FutureTECH, 08 Jul 2024) and Pre-Seed (Sanabil 500 MENA Seed Accelerator, 11 Nov 2024), amounts undisclosed.
register_entries.results: No independent evaluation was found. All available sources are the company's own marketing site, directory/startup-database listings and a third-party API profile that explicitly notes Cultivaet "publishes only a marketing site (cultivaet.ai) with no public API, developer portal, documentation". No adoption, yield, income or accuracy outcomes are documented anywhere in these sources.

register_entries.name: Qamhawey
uc: AI chat advisory ("Ask the Expert") answering crop care, pest management and planting questions via text, speech or uploaded images
Crop disease, pest and nutrient-deficiency detection from photos taken in the field
Weather forecasting (stated as 10 days ahead) with guidance on adapting farm operations to weather
Speech-to-text and text-to-speech in local Egyptian Arabic dialects for low-literacy farmers
Multimedia agricultural advisory content, product recommendations, and market price/supply-chain information
Linked e-commerce shop (shop.qamhawey.com) selling fertilisers, pesticides, seeds, seedlings, soil and equipment, with buy-now-pay-later instalments
register_entries.scale: Vendor claims: "actively supporting 50,000+ Egyptian farmers" and AI models "trained on a dataset of 800,000+ plant disease images" (Mahaseel LinkedIn post, 2025); the qamhawey.com site claims "10K+ Happy Farmers" and "5+ Years Experience" (with several other counters displaying as zero); the Mahaseel Masr shop 'About Us' page claims "+ 57,000" farmers, "+2,000,000" tonnes harvested and "530,000" hectares. The iOS app (Mahaseel Masr, version 1.0.4, 10/11/2025) shows only 1 rating. All figures are self-reported by the company and are mutually inconsistent.
register_entries.results: No independent evaluation found. All performance figures in the available sources are vendor self-claims from company-controlled web properties (e.g. "40% Crop Yield Increase", "35% Cost Reduction", "95% Disease Prevention", "95% Accuracy Rate") with no stated methodology, sample, or third-party verification. No peer-reviewed study, donor evaluation or randomised assessment of Qamhawey appears in these sources.
register_entries.src: Mahaseel (LinkedIn post): "Mahaseel's Qamhawey: AI for Egyptian Farmers"

international_pointers.statement: India's Digital Agriculture Mission illustrates one published approach to targeting and sequencing beneficiaries: rather than aiming at all farmers at once, it sets explicit, year-by-year coverage targets for issuing digital farmer identities, and it piloted the approach in six named districts across six states before scaling. Drafters of Chapter 3 may wish to look at how this phased, numerically-specified beneficiary ramp-up was expressed alongside a parallel geographic phasing of the Digital Crop Survey (400 districts in FY 2024-25, all districts in FY 2025-26).
international_pointers.quote: Creating digital identities for 11 crore farmers over three years (6 crore in FY 2024-25, 3 crore in FY 2025-26, and 2 crore in FY 2026-27)
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 3 must decide which farmer segments and regions come first and how many people each use case is meant to reach. This source shows a government stating beneficiary volumes per fiscal year and a district-by-district geographic rollout, with prior pilots in six named districts — a concrete template for how targeting and phasing can be written down and made measurable, independent of whether the same numbers or sequencing would suit Egypt.
international_pointers.source_name: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare — "Digital Agriculture Mission: Tech for Transforming Farmers' Lives"

international_pointers.statement: Kenya has published a draft national policy on agricultural data, information and digital systems that places the creation of an enabling legal, policy and institutional framework at the centre of its digital agriculture reform agenda — a drafting approach Egyptian drafters may wish to examine when specifying legal and regulatory actions under the policy and safeguards pillar.
international_pointers.quote: Central to this Policy is equally the establishment of an enabling legal, policy and institutional framework to support the effective roll out and governance of digital agricultural innovations.
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 6 must convert pillar-level safeguards into concrete reform and legal drafting tasks. The Kenyan draft is a published example of a government treating the legal, policy and institutional framework as a core policy component rather than an annex, and of framing that framework as a precondition for rolling out and governing digital agricultural innovations (data governance, interoperability, cyber security are named alongside it). It is offered only as a pointer to how another country structured such provisions; it is not a recommendation, not a ranking, and no claim is made that it would suit Egypt. Drafters should also note the document is explicitly a DRAFT dated March 2026 and reflects Kenya's devolved national/county governance structure, which differs from Egypt's.
international_pointers.source_name: Draft Kenya Agricultural Data, Information and Digital Policy, Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development (Kenya)

international_pointers.statement: India's Digital Agriculture Mission publishes its foundational digital-identity build as a phased, multi-year target sequence with annual volumes attached, which drafters may look at as one published way of expressing sequencing inside an investment program.
international_pointers.quote: Creating digital identities for 11 crore farmers over three years (6 crore in FY 2024-25, 3 crore in FY 2025-26, and 2 crore in FY 2026-27)
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 4 needs candidates expressed as sequenced items rather than an undated wish list. This is a published example where a farmer-registry component carries explicit year-by-year volume targets, and the same document pairs it with a second phased track (the Digital Crop Survey rolling from 400 districts to all districts) and names State Governments/Union Territories as the bodies that create and maintain the IDs  uiltner and a build order that drafters can inspect. It is a pointer only; the source describes India's institutional arrangements, not Egypt's.
international_pointers.source_name: Digital Agriculture Mission: Tech for Transforming Farmers' Lives (Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare, Press Information Bureau)

international_pointers.statement: Kenya's draft national agricultural data and digital policy assigns delivery roles across two tiers of government: the national government holds strategic leadership, coordination and policy guidance, while county governments — the frontline service deliverers — are to be enabled through common standards, capacity development and sustainable financing to participate in the national digital agriculture ecosystem. Drafters may wish to consider how such an explicit split of mandate between a central steward and sub-national delivery bodies is documented in that country's policy, alongside its stated intent to establish an enabling legal, policy and institutional framework for governing digital agricultural innovations. Note the document is a March 2026 draft, not an adopted instrument.
international_pointers.quote: On one hand, the national government will provide strategic leadership, coordination and policy guidance. On the other hand, county governments that are at the frontline of agricultural service delivery are to be empowered through common standards, capacity development, and sustainable financing mechanisms to fully participate in and benefit from the national digital agriculture ecosystem.
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 7 must state who owns the roadmap and where it sits institutionally. This is a published example of a country writing down the division of mandate between a national steward (strategic leadership, coordination, policy guidance) and sub-national implementers, plus the enabling conditions — common standards, capacity development, sustainable financing — that the policy says are needed for the lower tier to deliver. It offers drafters concrete language for describing steering arrangements and the capacity of the institutional home, without implying the same arrangement suits Egypt.
international_pointers.source_name: Draft Kenya Agricultural Data, Information and Digital Policy, Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development

international_pointers.statement: Kenya's draft national agricultural data, information and digital policy embeds climate responsiveness as one of the founding principles of the whole digital agriculture framework, rather than treating climate services as a separate programme — one option drafters could consider when deciding where climate alignment sits in the Egyptian roadmap's architecture.
international_pointers.quote: It articulates a farmer-centred, inclusive and devolved approach founded on strong data governance, interoperability, cyber security, innovation and climate responsiveness.
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 8 must decide whether climate alignment is a stand-alone chapter of activities or a cross-cutting design requirement on every data system and advisory channel. Kenya's draft policy shows one published way of doing the latter: climate responsiveness is listed alongside data governance, interoperability and cyber security as a foundation of the national digital agriculture framework, which in principle makes weather and climate data a shared public layer that advisory, subsidy and early-warning services all draw on. The same document notes that climate services already exist among Kenya's digital initiatives but that their potential has been constrained by fragmentation and limited interoperability — the specific failure mode a cross-cutting principle is meant to address. This is a pointer to an approach, not evidence that it has produced results, and not a recommendation for Egypt.
international_pointers.source_name: Draft Kenya Agricultural Data, Information and Digital Policy, Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development

international_pointers.statement: Kenya published a dedicated sector-level monitoring and evaluation framework that sits underneath its Climate-Smart Agriculture strategy and implementation framework, defining the framework's purpose as checking whether the implementation framework's objectives, outcomes and outputs are proceeding as planned — an example of anchoring a results chain in a pre-existing statutory reporting duty (the Climate Change Act 2016) rather than creating a standalone monitoring exercise.
international_pointers.quote: This monitoring and evaluation framework (M&EF) for CSA has been developed to foster the effective transformation of the agricultural sector toward resilient, low-carbon development, and to check whether the implementation of the KCSAIF objectives, outcomes, and outputs are proceeding as planned, in order to support optimal planning and efficiency in the utilization of resources.
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 9 needs results chains with baselines and a stated cadence for what is watched. Kenya's approach is a pointer on two structural choices drafters may wish to weigh: (1) issuing the M&E framework as a separate document subordinate to the strategy and its implementation framework, so indicators can be revised without reopening the strategy; and (2) tying the monitoring obligation to an existing legal reporting duty — the source notes the Climate Change Act 2016 obligates state departments and national government entities to report on sectoral emissions and on 'the performance and implementation of climate change duties and functions' and to 'regularly monitor and review the performance of the integrated climate change functions through sectoral mandates'. That linkage is one way to give a measurement register a mandatory reporting rhythm and named accountable entities instead of relying on project goodwill. Note the limits of this pointer: it is a climate-smart agriculture framework, not a digital agriculture one, its indicator content is not visible in the excerpt available here, and the document itself records that it was finalized with donor and CGIAR technical support — so the sustainability of the arrangement after external funding ends is not evidenced.
international_pointers.source_name: Kenya Climate-Smart Agriculture Monitoring and Evaluation Framework, Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Cooperatives (Government of Kenya)

international_pointers.statement: India's Telangana state published a draft Agricultural Data Management Policy (July 2022) that pairs the efficiency goal of data sharing with an explicit rights-protection objective, and structures the policy around named safeguard clauses — classification of the purpose of processing agricultural data containing personal data, de-identification and anonymization, access control, quality of datasets, compliance requirements, and a dedicated 'Grievance redressal' section (Clause 10) plus a Data Governance Framework (Clause 11). It was released for public consultation with a stated comment deadline and a prescribed submission template. Drafters of Chapter 10 may wish to look at how this document ties data rights and redress into the same instrument that authorises data sharing, and at the consultation mechanism used to surface objections before adoption.
international_pointers.quote: The objective of the Telangana Agricultural Data Management Policy 2022 (Policy) is to ensure that agricultural data is managed efficiently for the advancement of the agriculture sector, always protecting the rights of individuals.
international_pointers.why_it_matters: Chapter 10 covers data rights, consent and redress. This source is one published example in which a government instrument that enables agricultural data sharing simultaneously names the safeguards in its own table of contents — purpose classification for personal data, de-identification/anonymization, access control, dataset quality, compliance, grievance redressal and a data governance framework — rather than deferring them to later guidance. It also documents a concrete consultation route (fixed deadline, prescribed comment template, named receiving officials), which is relevant to the political-economy risk of adopting data rules without a recorded objection process. Note the caveats: this is a draft, not an enacted policy; it is sub-national and expressly stated to be 'subject to, and superseded by' state and central law; and the sources here do not show what was finally adopted or how redress performed in practice. Offered as a pointer for drafters to examine, not as a recommendation, ranking, or any claim about applicability to Egypt.
international_pointers.source_name: Draft Telangana Agricultural Data Management Policy 2022 (Agriculture & Cooperation Department, Government of Telangana) — draft released for public consultation
